*What did you do?*

I ran our project benchmarks and there was quite a bit of regression in some calculating code(among others).  
original issue <https://github.com/grafana/k6/issues/2116|grafana/k6#2116>  
repo to reproduce it with a lot less of the code: <https://github.com/MStoykov/reproduceScaleRegression|https://github.com/MStoykov/reproduceScaleRegression>

```
name                                    old time/op  new time/op   delta
ExecutionSegmentScale/5523-8            5.77ns ± 4%  10.45ns ± 2%   +81.15%  (p=0.000 n=9+10)
ExecutionSegmentScale/67280421310721-8  10.9ns ± 5%   59.9ns ± 7%  +451.72%  (p=0.000 n=10+10)
ExecutionSegmentScaleEmpty/5523-8       2.84ns ± 5%   0.64ns ± 7%   -77.32%  (p=0.000 n=10+10)

```

As mentioned in the repo the commit that makes the particular function inline is adb467ffd2d82b796de12bdd8effa2cfefe01f29 , but even without it, it's possible to make the code inline which results in the same regression even with go1.16.7.

Given that

*What did you expect to see?*

I would've wanted all the benchmarks to get faster :P.

In this particular example, I would expect that inlining will help not hinder, and some nice people in slack were theorizing that it's likely unaligned jumps or cache line misses and also (and most likely) the branch predictor getting hash collisions as proposed in <https://github.com/golang/go/issues/18977#issuecomment-301513260|golang/go#18977 (comment)> , but I don't know enough to confirm or deny any of this  
Given that there isn't such a regression in <https://github.com/grafana/k6/issues/2116#issuecomment-907331515|arm64 benchmarks results>, provided by <https://github.com/vearutop|@vearutop> :bow:

*What did you see instead?*

I saw a decrease in performance after a change that should've done the opposite.
